source: Parsons and Shukla (2025) Beyond Problem Solving: Framing and Problem-Solution Co-Evolution in Data Visualization Design (arXiv 2508.07058; IEEE TVCG 2026)
finding: Eleven expert visualization designers did one shared design challenge, kept diaries, and were interviewed. Reflexive thematic analysis found framing is not a front-loaded step. Designers moved between understanding the problem and building solutions throughout, and sketching or prototyping was used to understand the problem, not only to refine the answer.
numbers: N=11 experts (years of experience bands 2-5, 6-10, 11+); interviews ranged 7 to 87 minutes; recruited from March 2023; USD 250 each. Qualitative themes only, no effect sizes.
limits: Eleven people, one contrived time-bounded challenge, self-report diaries and retrospective interviews, researcher-interpreted themes. Shows co-evolution is reported by experts, not that it causes better outcomes.
agent_relevance: Supports a loop where an attempt can change the problem statement. Gives no evidence about which order wins.

source: Parsons and Shukla (2025) Beyond Problem Solving (same paper), reframing triggers
finding: Reframes were prompted by solution-side events: tool limits, time pressure, a chart type that failed to show patterns, or a metaphor that suggested a new angle. Participants named framing tools (metaphors, heuristics, scoping, values) and said a compelling early frame can persist and steer later choices.
numbers: Reported as participant vignettes (for example one designer dropped a granular view after a solution attempt failed to clarify patterns). No counts of reframes per participant given in the text I read.
limits: Vignettes were chosen for richness and clarity by the authors, so they may overstate how common reframing is.
agent_relevance: Matches guardrail G1/G2: reframe on a signal from a real failing output, not on a schedule.

source: Team conceptual design protocol study (Applied Sciences 2020, 10(18):6303) Revisiting Problem-Solution Co-Evolution in the Context of Team Conceptual Design Activity
finding: Protocol analysis of four teams of three engineering students, using an analysis-synthesis-evaluation state-transition code split by problem space versus solution space. Ideation spent a large share on the problem space; concept review was almost all solution space.
numbers: N=12 students in 4 teams; two 50-minute team activities (ideation, concept review) re-used from Cash et al.; mean coded segments per team 333 (ideation) and 313 (review); ideation transitions 49% synthesis, 32% analysis, 19% evaluation; ideation 37% problem-space and 63% solution-space; review 44% analysis, 31% synthesis, 25% evaluation, 12% problem and 88% solution. Inter-rater event-alignment kappa 0.71 on 20% of the data.
limits: Eight sessions only; sessions cut into 24 thirds that are treated as independent although they are not; verbal protocols only; students, one task (camera mount on a balloon).
agent_relevance: Gives a base rate: even in an exploratory phase, about a third of moves touched the problem. A budget share for problem-side moves (S2) can be set from this, though it is weak evidence.

source: Team conceptual design protocol study (Appl. Sci. 2020, 10, 6303), hypothesis tests on analysis/synthesis/evaluation versus problem/solution
finding: The textbook mapping (analysis equals problem space, synthesis equals solution space) was not supported. Analysis correlated negatively with problem-related transitions; synthesis-heavy fragments carried MORE problem-related talk. Only evaluation matched (more solution-related). The correlations vanished when ideation and review were analysed separately.
numbers: Spearman rS(22) = -0.649, p<0.001 (analysis vs problem-related); strong negative correlation synthesis vs solution-related; rS(22) = 0.672, p<0.001 (evaluation vs solution-related). 24 data points. H1a and H1b not supported; H1c supported.
limits: Correlations hold only on the pooled data of both activity types (a between-activity effect); non-independent fragments inflate significance.
agent_relevance: Warning: the problem/solution distinction cannot be read off the operator type. Our code should tag problem versus solution entities explicitly, not infer them from verbs like analyse or generate.

source: Team conceptual design protocol study (Appl. Sci. 2020, 10, 6303), transitions between spaces
finding: Overall, new problem entities (new requirements or constraints) were more likely to appear right after solution-space work than after problem-space work. This reversed during ideation, where problem entities more often followed problem-space work. New solution entities mostly followed solution-space work, so the claimed symmetric two-way co-evolution was only half supported.
numbers: Wilcoxon, paired per fragment: new problem entities after solution vs problem space p<0.05 (overall only); new solution entities after solution vs problem space p<0.001 (overall and within each activity). Analysis-then-synthesis most probable sequence (AA vs AS p=0.002; AS vs AE p<0.001); evaluation followed by synthesis not clearly more likely than evaluation followed by analysis.
limits: Same small data set; the problem-after-solution result depends on the activity type; authors call for larger samples.
agent_relevance: Evidence for the direction that matters to us: solution attempts are the main source of new problem knowledge (supports S3 to S2 feedback). The reverse direction, problem work seeding solutions, is weaker.

source: Halstrom and Galle (2015) Design as Co-Evolution of Problem, Solution, and Audience, Artifact 3(4)
finding: Conceptual paper with three case examples. It accepts co-evolution of problem and solution as a common phenomenon but states it is not a defining feature of design and does not always occur, even in non-trivial cases. It argues the 'muddle through' reading should be replaced by explicit rational deliberation about the problem. Adds a third co-evolving element, the audience.
numbers: Three cases (one student degree project plus two professional examples); no quantitative data. Authors note empirical support for the audience claim is hard to come by.
quote: co-evolution does not always occur in design, not even in all non-trivial cases
limits: Cases picked on purpose to show the pattern; one informant interviewed for the student case; authors are part of the same school as the student.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: co-evolution is a tendency, not a law. Our scaffold should not force a problem-restating step on tasks whose goal is already fixed and checkable.

source: Design science research ethnography, IEEE Trans. Eng. Management (2023, PMC10062208) Search and Evaluation of Coevolving Problem and Solution Spaces in a Complex Healthcare Design Scenario
finding: Eight-year ethnography of one research project (IT support for chronic wounds). Standard define-then-build methods fit poorly because the problem was new and ill-defined. The team found that treating the work as search over co-evolving problem and solution spaces worked better, and that evaluation should change purpose (learn about the spaces, not only grade an artifact).
numbers: One project over eight years, several design science sub-projects; no sample statistics. The authors cite Dorst and Cross (2001) as consistent.
limits: Single case, self-study by the team that did the work; no comparison condition; in their own words, an 'invention quadrant' problem, so it may not transfer to routine design.
agent_relevance: Moderator: co-evolution framing is reported as most useful for new problems with no known solution, not for routine ones. Could gate S2/S3 looping on a novelty or impasse signal.

source: Guo, Yin, Sun and Chen (2025) How Generative AI supports human in conceptual design, Design Science (arXiv 2502.00283)
finding: Twenty novice designers in four groups (human only, ChatGPT, Midjourney, both) did two design tasks. Participants in AI groups said AI helped most in idea generation, problem definition and idea evolution; evaluation and selection stayed human-led. Expert ratings of final designs differed by group for novelty, cost and overall score.
numbers: N=20 (15 in AI groups); stages helped: idea generation 86.7%, problem definition 73.3%, idea evolution 60%; evaluation/selection judged human-led by 86.7%. Expert rating group differences: novelty p<0.01, cost p<0.01, overall p=0.005; feasibility p=0.084, usability p=0.228, functional diversity p=0.422 (not significant). Rater Cohen kappa 0.66 among five raters.
limits: Five participants per group, novices, self-reported helping stages, multiple tests without stated correction in the text I read; ChatGPT users needed solution-oriented prompts at the problem-definition stage.
agent_relevance: Humans handed problem definition and idea generation to the model but kept selection. That supports code or an outside check doing selection (G5) while the model drafts problem framings.

source: Guo, Yin, Sun and Chen (2024) Empirical Study of Problem-solution Co-evolution in Human-GAI Collaborative Conceptual Design, DRS2024
finding: Retrospective protocol analysis of twenty novice designers co-designing with text and image generative AI. The authors propose a human-GAI co-evolution model in which AI helps humans explore problem framing, and say AI may raise team creativity by fostering abductive reasoning.
numbers: N=20 novices. Abstract page only: no scores or effect sizes were available to me.
limits: Only the abstract and metadata were read (full PDF returned 403). Treat claims as unverified beyond the abstract. Likely the same data set as the Design Science paper above.
agent_relevance: Only direct 'co-evolution plus generative AI' empirical title I found; its numbers are not checked.

source: Chen et al (2026) Generative AI as a cognitive support tool in early-stage design ideation: a human-AI co-ideation experiment, PLOS ONE (PMC13585246)
finding: Within-subject, counterbalanced test of AI-assisted (text plus image) versus human-only brainstorming on one brief. AI-assisted output scored much higher on problem framing and mechanism breadth, but human-only output scored higher on innovation and on proposed solution strategies. No robust difference in the refined design.
numbers: N=32 design undergraduates, 3 expert raters, six rubric criteria, Holm-Bonferroni within family. Problem framing human 2.94 vs AI 4.64, t(31)=14.03, dz=2.48; mechanism 2.99 vs 4.48, dz=2.49; evaluator perspective dz=1.53; creator perspective dz=0.90; innovation human 4.66 vs AI 3.40, dz=2.69; solution strategies 4.22 vs 3.67, dz=1.47. No difference on 5 design attributes after correction.
limits: Output formats differed (sketches vs generated text/images) so raters could identify the condition; carryover from using the same brief twice; rubric criteria not independent; one Taiwanese school, one product task; no objective ideation measure. Effects of d near 2.5 are probably rater halo.
agent_relevance: Better problem framing did not produce better solutions or novelty here. Warns against assuming that a richer problem statement from the model improves the final answer; measure it with a code check.

source: Frontiers in Psychology (2026) Effects of integrating a structured design thinking strategy into generative AI-supported design learning (PMC13318989)
finding: A Double Diamond (discover-define-develop-deliver, problem then solution diamonds) structure added to GAI-supported design classes raised design achievement over GAI without the structure and over traditional teaching.
numbers: N=120 undergraduates, 40 per group (GAI with structured design thinking, GAI alone, traditional). Design achievement post-test means 20.90 (SD 7.64), 18.65 (7.41), 16.13 (6.85); one-way ANOVA F=43.28, p<0.001. ANCOVA on creative self-efficacy reported F=803.16 (very large, suspicious).
limits: Course-level quasi-experiment; the structure is a bundle (problem-first then solution), so it cannot separate problem-first order from just having any structure; outcome-based and self-report measures; the F=803 value looks implausible and was not explained in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Weak support that explicit problem-then-solution scaffolding helps novices using AI. It does not test co-evolution against problem-first.

source: Carichon et al (2026) IDEAFix: Evaluation Framework for Creative Defixation Prompting in LLMs (arXiv 2606.00875)
finding: Large controlled test of how task framing changes LLM idea generation. Brief type and the surprise or negativity of an attribute keyword shifted novelty, rarity and diversity (all statistically significant), so how the problem is framed changes the solution space the model searches.
numbers: 14,350 prompts; 5 models (Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen3-30B, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o, Grok-4.1-fast); 3 runs each; temperature 0.7 or 1.0. Product briefs gave highest novelty and rarity, service briefs lowest. Surprising keywords raised novelty and rarity but lowered diversity; surprising-negative combinations gave the most novel output. Model means: novelty 0.428 (GPT) to 0.556 (Llama); fluency 9.35 (Llama) to 20.16 (Grok).
limits: Novelty is embedding distance from a control set, not human judgment; no solution quality or feasibility scored; single-shot generation, no feedback loop.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence that the problem statement is a lever on the solution distribution. Supports trying several problem framings, but only the novelty axis is measured.

source: Carichon et al (2026) IDEAFix, prompting strategies including Design Thinking reframing
finding: All 25 method-inspired prompts beat the control prompts on the creativity metrics. A Design Thinking prompt that told the model to reframe the problem as a How Might We statement before generating did not beat simpler prompts. Brainstorming prompts and a hand-made AI-specific prompt ('think outside the box', 'wild') scored best; C-K theory and SCAMPER prompts did not necessarily raise novelty.
numbers: Gains in the top-5 ideas over the mean for the best alternative of each method read from Figure 4b ranged from roughly +10% to +41% (figure text is garbled in the PDF extraction). Differences versus control significant by t-tests (Table 9, appendix not opened).
quote: gains in novelty may be more closely associated with the explicitness of divergence instructions than with the underlying structure of the creativity method
limits: One-pass prompting: the reframe step happens inside one generation with no check of the new frame. Metrics are semantic distance only.
agent_relevance: Null-ish evidence for in-prompt reframing as a novelty booster. Matches our earlier schema finding that LLM reframing without a check gives little.

source: Carichon et al (2026) IDEAFix, homogenization
finding: Even with defixation prompts, the five models gave solutions that stayed in a shared semantic region, heavily digital and technological. Cross-model distances were small.
numbers: Pairwise model novelty distances in Figure 5a between 0.206 and 0.341 on a 0 to 1 cosine scale; authors call this an LLM hivemind effect.
limits: Embedding space choice affects distances; no human baseline run in the same design.
agent_relevance: Reframing the problem moves individual ideas but not the shared region, so frames from the same model family are correlated (G4).

source: Xu, Martelaro and McComb (2026) Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design (arXiv 2603.24768)
finding: On a battery pack design task, an agent loop where a second agent monitors progress (improving, stalling, regressing) and pushes it out of fixation gave better designs than a plain retry loop or self-monitoring, at the same number of steps.
numbers: Gemini 3.1 Pro, 30 runs per system. Mean capacity (Ah): plain loop 72.07 (SD 20.52, 29/30 valid), self-regulation 106.08 (SD 45.60), co-regulation 141.17 (SD 48.45). ANOVA F(2,86)=21.606, p<0.001, partial eta squared 0.334. Plain vs self d=0.956; plain vs co-regulation d=1.846 (p<0.001); self vs co-regulation d=0.746 (p=0.005). Steps taken did not differ, F(2,87)=0.031, p=0.97.
limits: One design problem with a numeric objective, one model, runs share a base seed, high variance in the better arms; not specifically a problem-reframing test.
agent_relevance: Closest agent test of the S2/S3 loop with a progress monitor: an external signal of stalling plus a nudge to change approach beat blind iteration at equal cost. Supports signal-triggered doubt (G1) over scheduled doubt.

source: Wang et al (2026) NexusAI: Design Space Exploration of Ideas through Cognitive Abstraction and Functional Decomposition (arXiv 2604.10575)
finding: A tool that breaks LLM ideas into typed fragments and lets users move between abstraction levels led to more branching exploration and less workload than a baseline LLM interface in a within-subject study.
numbers: N=14 within-subject; Wilcoxon signed-rank. Average out-degree per node 0.98 vs 0.30 (p=0.004); re-engagement with core nodes 0.367 vs 0.097 (p=0.008); NASA-TLX overall 3.26 vs 4.17 (p=0.049); frustration 2.43 vs 4.36 (p=0.006).
limits: N=14, many tests with p near 0.05 and no stated correction, self-report plus interaction logs, not solution quality.
agent_relevance: Structured typed representation of fragments aids exploration, in line with a typed problem-frame record, but the evidence is thin.

source: Engineering design hackathon, ChatGPT 4.0 versus graduate students (arXiv 2404.18479) ChatGPT as an inventor
finding: In a 48-hour prototyping hackathon, ChatGPT 4.0 directed two human executors. It ranked second among six teams and produced strong concepts. It gave up promising concepts after minor difficulties, added needless complexity, and showed design fixation. Communication with participants was hampered by vague descriptions.
numbers: Dataset of more than 100 prototypes; LLM team second of six.
limits: One run of one LLM team; humans acted as the hands, which adds noise; abstract and introduction read in detail, not the full results.
agent_relevance: Shows both failure modes our loop must manage: premature abandonment of a good direction after a small failure, and fixation on one direction. A reframe-on-failure rule needs a check that the failure is real.

source: Deng, Zhang, Chen and Gu (2024) Rephrase and Respond (arXiv 2311.04205)
finding: Letting the model restate the question before answering raised GPT-4 accuracy a lot on tasks where the original wording was ambiguous. This is a problem-restatement-before-solving effect.
numbers: GPT-4, 10 tasks. Average zero-shot accuracy 64.95 (original) vs 89.77 for the main RaR prompt; four prompt variants 87.17 to 88.97. Examples: Last-letter (4) 21.36 to 86.82; coin flip 74.55 to 99.09; Dates 69.92 to 75.88; CSQA 84.09 to 85.45. Chinese Idiom 32.38 to 35.24 (small; zero-shot CoT was 31.43). StereoSet language modelling 84.09 to 97.73.
limits: Largest gains where the question was badly worded for the model; small where the task was well posed. Tasks are single-answer puzzles, not open design.
agent_relevance: Restating the problem BEFORE solving helps when the prompt is ambiguous. Our schema's 'restate after a failed attempt' versus 'before' question (SUBFIELDS item 2) is still untested here; RaR only tests before.

source: Deng et al (2024) Rephrase and Respond, model-size boundary
finding: Gains from self-rephrasing depend on model strength. GPT-4 gained most; GPT-3.5 and Vicuna-13b gained less and on some tasks (Sports) got slightly worse. A rephrase by a stronger model helped the weaker one more than its own rephrase.
numbers: Two-step RaR with Vicuna-13b: its own rephrases vs GPT-4 rephrases improved on several tasks; one task column read 5.45 (self) vs 10.45 (GPT-4-rephrased); another 58.10 vs 61.90.
limits: Table column labels were scrambled in text extraction; only the direction and rough size should be trusted.
agent_relevance: The model that restates the problem should not be weaker than the one that solves it. A frame is only as good as the framer.

source: Zheng et al (2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs (arXiv 2310.06117)
finding: First asking the model for the underlying principle or higher-level question, then solving, raised PaLM-2L accuracy on physics, chemistry and time-sensitive QA more than chain of thought did. This is a model-run reframing step before solving.
numbers: PaLM-2L baseline MMLU Physics 66.4%, Chemistry 70.9%; with step-back 73.2% and 81.8% (CoT 65% and 75.3%). TimeQA 41.5% to 66% (RAG 57.4%); SituatedQA 54.3% to 57.5%. Step-back fixes up to about 40% of baseline errors and introduces at most about 12% new ones.
limits: Gains vary a lot by task; most remaining errors come from the reasoning step itself; gains on the physics set were similar to or smaller than for chemistry.
agent_relevance: Best positive LLM result for abstracting the problem before solving. Note it is front-loaded abstraction, the problem-first side of the debate.

source: Goel (2018) Cognitive Neuroscience of Design Creativity review (PMC6236478)
finding: The review states that design problem framing continues throughout the task (co-evolution) and cites studies finding that designers who spend more time structuring the problem later make better creative solutions, while skipping the problem-setting stage or spending too long or defining it too rigidly can hurt. It credits a vague initial problem formulation as a source of creativity.
numbers: Cites Atman et al (1999, freshman vs senior engineers) and Goel and Grafman (2000). No new data in this review.
limits: Secondary source; it states an inverted-U (not too little, not too much) without a measured optimum; Atman 1999 is correlational and compares students at different years.
agent_relevance: Supports an inverted-U for problem-framing effort. A cap on S2 budget is more defensible than 'always map the problem first' or 'never map it'.

source: Goel (2014) Creative brains: designing in the real world, Frontiers in Human Neuroscience (PMC4012206)
finding: Case study of an architect with right frontal damage versus a matched control architect redesigning the same lab space. The control moved from abstract kernel ideas through related drawings to detail. The patient's preliminary drawings were fragmentary and unrelated, and his kernel idea appeared two-thirds of the way in. The paper argues design needs both lateral (broadening) and vertical (deepening) transformations of the problem space.
numbers: N=1 patient, N=1 control; control had nine states (start, 7 intermediate, goal), patient had five (3 intermediate); fMRI design vs non-design task: mean completion 36 s vs 31.8 s, more right dorsolateral prefrontal activity in design.
limits: Single patient; tied to a lesion; verbal protocol analysis; far from LLM agents.
agent_relevance: Only suggestive: a missing ability to hold a coherent problem-level kernel while exploring fragments can break the process. Our typed frame record is a way to externalise that kernel.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution, Design Studies 22(5):425-437
finding: Re-analysis of protocols of industrial designers from the 1994 Delft Protocols Workshop (a train litter-disposal task). Creative moments were linked to a 'bridge' where a problem frame and a partial solution fit each other. Not opened this session (publisher blocked; Crossref has no abstract).
numbers: From memory, not verified: small set of professional designers (about nine protocols in the workshop), a single task; no inferential statistics. Cited by about 1,570 works (Crossref, 2026).
limits: Qualitative case reading of a handful of protocols, no comparison condition, no test of whether co-evolution produced better outcomes than other orders. Critics (see b06, b07) note it is not universal.
agent_relevance: Founding claim. Treat as hypothesis-generating. Verify numbers from the PDF before quoting.

source: Maher and Poon (1996) Modeling design exploration as co-evolution; Poon and Maher (1997) Co-evolution and emergence in design
finding: Computational model: a genetic algorithm in which the fitness function (the problem) and the design solutions both change during search. It formalised 'exploration' as search plus change of the problem space. Not opened (publisher access).
numbers: No human data. Crossref citation counts 197 (1996 paper) and 64 (1997 paper).
limits: A model, not evidence that human designers behave this way; claims of better results over fixed-goal search depend on toy design tasks.
agent_relevance: A formal precedent for an agent that edits its own objective during search. Our G2/G3 guards (revise only from real output; check on something not fitted to) address the risk that the objective drifts to fit the solutions.

source: Wiltschnig, Christensen and Ball (2013) Collaborative problem-solution co-evolution in creative design, Design Studies 34(5)
finding: Protocol study of collaborative designers; reported (from memory, unverified) that co-evolution in teams is driven by questions and clarifications between members and that problem and solution episodes alternate. Not opened (publisher blocked).
numbers: Not verified. Cited by about 155 works (Crossref).
limits: Qualitative; small team sample; cannot say whether co-evolution improved the product.
agent_relevance: Suggests the trigger for problem-side moves is a question or clash between viewpoints, which maps to disagreement between attempts (G1 signal), not to a timer.

source: Kokotovich (2008) Problem analysis and thinking tools: an empirical study of non-hierarchical mind mapping, Design Studies 29(1):49-69
finding: Empirical study of designers using non-hierarchical mind maps to analyse a design problem before solving; basis for the critique that mapping the problem space first may serve creativity better than muddling through. Only the abstract page of a later Kokotovich paper was opened in the earlier SUBFIELDS file. Not opened here.
numbers: Not verified. Cited by about 100 works (Crossref).
limits: I could not check sample size, comparison, or effect size; do not quote a number from this entry.
agent_relevance: The main rival to co-evolution; a controlled problem-first versus interleaved comparison on an LLM agent with equal tokens is the discriminating experiment and is still missing.

source: Atman et al (2007) Engineering design processes: a comparison of students and expert practitioners, J. Engineering Education 96(4):359-379
finding: From memory and from the citation context in b01 and b21, not opened: experts spent a larger share of time on problem scoping and information gathering than students and produced higher quality designs; students tended to start generating solutions early. This is the best-known observational evidence for 'more problem scoping goes with better designs'.
numbers: Not verified (I recall roughly 20 to 30 students per group and a handful of experts; do not cite).
limits: Correlational and confounded by expertise, task familiarity and time spent; does not show that mapping the problem first causes better results.
agent_relevance: The expertise confound is the key moderator: experts differ in many ways, so copying their scoping share is not shown to help a model.

source: Suwa, Gero and Purcell (2000) Unexpected discoveries and S-invention of design requirements, Design Studies 21(6)
finding: Protocol study of architects' sketching. From memory, unverified: unexpected discoveries in sketches led designers to invent new requirements, a documented path from solution to problem. Not opened.
numbers: Not verified. Cited by about 222 works (Crossref).
limits: Few participants, exploratory sketch analysis, architects only.
agent_relevance: An independent source for the 'new problem entities come from solution attempts' direction that b05 found in teams.
